notes.meaning: Mary leaves the house right away to go to Jesus as soon as she hears He is calling for her. Her deep love for the Lord moved her to hurry to Him without hesitation.
Jesus had not yet entered Bethany, but waited outside where Martha had first met Him. Jewish burial places were kept outside villages, so staying there placed Jesus near Lazarus's tomb.

The friends who were consoling Mary thought she was rushing out to weep at her brother's tomb, so they followed her. Although they only meant to comfort her, God used their actions to bring a crowd of witnesses to the miracle about to take place.
Mary falls at Jesus' feet in deep sorrow and reverent honor. She repeats the very same words her sister had spoken, expressing her faith that Lazarus would not have died if Jesus had been there.
When Jesus saw Mary and the mourners weeping, He was deeply stirred within His spirit. He entered fully into human sorrow, proving that He is deeply touched by our grief.

differ.view: Jesus groaned because He was holding back His tears by an act of will, keeping His emotions under perfect control.
The groaning expresses holy anger and outrage at the painful reality of sin and death.

notes.meaning: Jesus asked where they had laid Lazarus, speaking gently as a man even though as God He already knew. They invited Him to come and see the place for Himself.
Jesus wept quiet tears of tender compassion on the way to the tomb. His tears show that He is truly human, and that it is natural and right for believers to grieve when facing loss.
The people watching noticed Jesus' tears and saw how deeply He cared for Lazarus. His visible sorrow showed the genuine warmth of His love.

Some onlookers questioned why a man who opened the eyes of the blind could not keep His friend from dying. Their words showed a strange mix of belief in His past miracles and doubt about His power over death.
Deeply moved again, Jesus arrived at the tomb. It was a cave cut into the rock, with a large stone laid across the entrance.
Jesus ordered the people to roll away the stone from the entrance. Martha objected because Lazarus had been dead four days, meaning decay had already set in and the body would have a terrible smell.
Jesus gently challenged Martha's doubts by pointing back to His promise. If she would put her trust in Him, she would see God's wonderful power and glory displayed.

After the stone was rolled away, Jesus looked up to heaven and thanked the Father for hearing Him. He did not need to ask for extra power, because He and the Father are always in perfect harmony, but He prayed aloud so the crowd would believe God had sent Him.
Jesus shouted with a loud and commanding voice for Lazarus to come out of the tomb. He spoke openly with divine authority, demonstrating that even death must obey His word.
Lazarus walked out of the tomb alive, with his hands and feet wrapped in linen strips and a cloth over his face. Jesus told the amazed bystanders to unwrap him so he could move freely.
Many of the Jews who had come to comfort Mary saw this undeniable miracle and placed their faith in Jesus. The raising of a man dead for four days proved to them that He was truly the Messiah.

Rather than putting their trust in Jesus, some of the witnesses went straight to the Pharisees to report what had happened. Their hardened hearts turned a wonderful work of God into an opportunity to oppose Him.

The chief priests and Pharisees called a meeting of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high council, alarmed by all the miraculous signs Jesus was performing. They feared that if everyone believed in Him, the Romans would suspect rebellion and destroy both their temple and their nation.

Caiaphas, the high priest that year, dismissed the council's hesitation and offered a purely political solution. He argued that it was far better for one man to die than for the entire Jewish people to be wiped out by Rome.

Caiaphas did not realize that God was guiding his words to speak a true prophecy. Because he held the sacred office of high priest, the Holy Spirit used him to declare that Jesus was about to die as an atonement, paying the penalty for the sins of the nation.

Jesus was to die not only for the Jewish people, but to gather all of God's scattered children across the world into one body. His death brings together people from every background into a single family of faith.

differ.view: The scattered children of God refers to the elect whom God has already chosen for salvation before they come to faith.
The phrase refers to all believers across every nation and age who will be gathered into the one church of Christ.

notes.meaning: From that moment on, the Jewish council firmly agreed on a plan to put Jesus to death. They stopped debating whether to act and focused on finding the best opportunity to kill Him.

Knowing their deadly plot, Jesus stopped traveling openly in Judea and withdrew with His disciples to the town of Ephraim near the wilderness. He stayed there quietly until the proper time came for Him to give His life.

As the Passover festival drew near, crowds of pilgrims traveled from the countryside up to Jerusalem. They arrived early to complete the washings and ceremonial cleansing required by the law before celebrating the feast.

While standing in the temple courts, the pilgrims kept looking for Jesus and wondering whether He would risk coming to the festival. Meanwhile, the chief priests and Pharisees had issued an official order that anyone who knew where He was must report Him so He could be arrested.
